P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, under Bank of Thailand rules. Anyone receiving USD 1 million (or equivalent) or more from abroad must repatriate it within 360 days and either sell it to an authorised bank or deposit it in a foreign-currency account with an authorised bank. Receipts below USD 1 million are exempt (Bank of Thailand; Baker McKenzie). Foreign currency received abroad can also be used directly for permitted obligations to non-residents. In December 2025 the Ministry of Finance and the BoT proposed raising the exemption to under USD 10 million (public hearing; adoption not confirmed) (Baker McKenzie).

sources.title: Exchange Control Regulation
sources.quote: Any person receiving foreign currencies from abroad in an amount equivalent to USD 1 million or above is required to repatriate such funds immediately within 360 days from the export date or the transaction date, and sell to an authorized bank or deposit them in a foreign currency account with an authorized bank within 360 days of receipt.

sources.title: Thailand: Advancing FX ecosystem reforms (December 2025)
sources.quote: The foreign currency received by a Thai resident outside Thailand is less than USD 1 million (or its equivalent in other currency).

sources.title: Thailand: Advancing FX ecosystem reforms (December 2025)
sources.quote: from less than USD 1 million (or its equivalent in other currency) to less than USD 10 million (or its equivalent in other currency).

P1_fx_receipts.notes: Supersedes the older USD 200,000 threshold in the earlier Tilleke source.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Residents may maintain foreign-currency deposit (FCD) accounts with authorised banks in Thailand, and repatriated foreign income can be deposited there instead of converted (Bank of Thailand).

sources.title: Exchange Control Regulation
sources.quote: Residents are allowed to maintain foreign currency deposit accounts (FCD) with authorized banks in Thailand.

P4_paypal.question: Can residents receive money via PayPal?
P4_paypal.answer: Yes, PayPal works for receiving and withdrawing in Thailand. You can withdraw to your Thai bank account in baht: the minimum is THB 360, withdrawals of THB 5,000 or more are free, and smaller ones carry a fee (THB 50 per the fee table). Withdrawals usually complete within 7 working days, and only local-currency transfers are supported, so withdrawing a foreign-currency balance incurs a conversion fee (PayPal Thailand help and fee pages). Thailand is still not on PayPal's Payouts list, so platforms that pay through PayPal Payouts may not reach Thai accounts.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: A sole proprietorship does not require official registration as a business entity (Board of Investment guide). Business entities are regulated by the Department of Business Development (DBD), and a commercial registration with the DBD is needed only for certain activities (Deel). You still need a taxpayer number from the Revenue Department, and VAT registration if above the threshold (see L2/L4). TRAP: generally only Thai nationals (or US citizens under the Amity Treaty) can own a sole proprietorship, and foreigners also need a work permit (Deel).

sources.quote: Step 1: Check your eligibility In Thailand, a sole proprietorship can generally only be registered by Thai nationals or by US citizens under the US-Thai Amity Treaty.

sources.quote: • Sole proprietorship and non-registered ordinary partnership: Do not require official registration.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: Official TIN description supplied by Thailand to the OECD: under Revenue Code s.3 decies, individual income taxpayers must have and use a Tax Identification Number. Individuals with assessable income must apply for a TIN and taxpayer card, in the Director-General's prescribed form, within 60 days of the date assessable income is first received (Revenue Department). Foreigners staying in Thailand 14 days or less are excluded.

sources.publisher: OECD AEOI portal (information supplied by Thailand's Revenue Department)
sources.title: Thailand — Information on Tax Identification Numbers (OECD)
sources.quote: Individuals with assessable income, ordinary partnerships or non-juristic bodies of persons, deceased persons, and undivided estates must submit an application for a TIN and taxpayer card in the form prescribed by the Director-General within 60 days from the date assessable income is received.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Thai residents are taxed on Thai-source income. Under Revenue Department Order Por. 161/2566, foreign-source income earned from 1 January 2024 is taxable when brought into Thailand, in the same or any later year. Before 2024 it was taxed only if remitted in the year it was earned. Personal income tax is progressive up to 35%.

sources.title: Thailand - Individual - Taxes on personal income
sources.quote: Residents who derive assessable income derived from outside Thailand would only be subject to tax if such income is earned in any tax year starting from 1 January 2024 onwards and is remitted to Thailand, wholly or partially, in the same or a later tax year.

sources.title: Thailand's Tax Policy Shift: Change In Foreign Source Income Tax Treatment For Thai Tax Resident
sources.quote: 161/2566, when a Thai tax resident repatriates offshore-sourced income into Thailand, that income will be subject to taxation in the year it is brought into Thailand, irrespective of the year in which it was initially earned.

sources.title: Thailand's Tax Policy Shift: Change In Foreign Source Income Tax Treatment For Thai Tax Resident
sources.quote: This represents a shift from the previous rule where only income brought into Thailand in the same year it was earned was subject to taxation.

L3_income_tax_foreign.notes: TRAP: 2024 change to remittance rule. Work physically performed in Thailand for foreign clients is likely Thai-source (not confirmed in captured text).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: Statutory VAT is 10%, currently reduced to 7% until 30 September 2027. Anyone regularly supplying goods or services in Thailand with annual turnover above THB 1.8 million must register (Revenue Department). Zero rate applies to exports of goods and to services rendered in Thailand and used outside Thailand, under conditions set by the Director-General. Freelance services for foreign clients can therefore be zero-rated if the conditions are met.

sources.quote: Taxable Person Any person or entity who regularly supplies goods or provides services in Thailand and has an annual turnover exceeding 1.8 million baht is subject to VAT in Thailand.

sources.quote: Value-added tax (VAT) The standard rate of VAT is 10%, but the rate is currently reduced to 7% until 30 September 2027 (unless further extended by the government).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) has been fully in force since 1 June 2022. The PDPC's Expert Committee handles complaints and can impose administrative fines. Small businesses are exempt from keeping a record of processing activities (ROPA, from 21 June 2022), except where processing is risky, regular or required by computer-crime law.

sources.title: Key developments in Thailand's PDPA regulations
sources.quote: Significant developments have unfolded since Thailand's Personal Data Protection Act took full effect 1 June 2022.

sources.title: Key developments in Thailand's PDPA regulations
sources.quote: The release of subordinate legislation, along with the legal interpretations of the Expert Committee — which is authorized to consider complaints, investigate and impose punitive measures — further enhanced the PDPA's effectiveness, as Thailand intensifies efforts to ensure the safety and security of personal data.

sources.title: First set of subordinate regulations enacted for Thailand's PDPA
sources.quote: The ROPA Exemption Notification came into force on June 21, 2022.

sources.title: First set of subordinate regulations enacted for Thailand's PDPA
sources.quote: This exemption will not apply to small businesses in certain circumstances, such as when the processing of personal data is required by law related to a computer crime to retain computer traffic data, when it involves personal data having a risk of affecting the rights and freedom of an individual, or when the data controller processes the personal data on a regular basis.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Under the Direct Sales and Direct Marketing Act, a consumer who buys through direct sales or direct marketing (including online) may terminate the contract by written notice within 7 days of receiving the goods or service (s. 33). The operator must give a purchase document in clear Thai stating the right to terminate, printed more conspicuously than the rest of the document (ss. 23, 30, 31) (Aster of Asia). Direct-marketing operators must register (search summary).

sources.quote: A consumer who buys through direct sales or direct marketing may terminate the contract by giving written notice within seven days from the date of receiving the goods or service.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.note: Single secondary domain (Aster of Asia summary of the Act) captured on 2026-10-25; the Act's official text was not captured.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving). Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (6) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
